title: Crash-safe write discipline is split: config.json, hosts CSV, and jobs.json bypass the atomic writer, and the .bak that Save maintains is never consulted on corrupt load
existing_state: The repo has one blessed crash-safe persistence path — JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic (temp file + File.Replace, Utilities/JsonFileWriter.cs:21) — and HistoryStorageService routes everything through it (HistoryStorageService.cs:739-740, used at 468/475). But the three other user-data files use bare truncate-and-write: config.json via File.WriteAllText (ConfigurationService.cs:144), the hosts CSV via a direct StreamWriter (CsvManager.cs:78, no backup at all), and jobs.json via File.WriteAllText (JobStorageService.cs:243). config.json is the single highest-value file in the app (entire preset library, all environments' host tables, compressed app state). The downstream machinery proves the cost of this split: Save pre-copies a .bak (ConfigurationService.cs:116-120) and Load has a whole corrupt-file recovery path (ConfigurationService.cs:91-102) — yet that recovery backs up the corrupt file and falls back to FACTORY DEFAULTS without ever attempting the known-good config.json.bak sitting next to it. So today a crash or power loss mid-save corrupts the live config, and on next start the user is silently reset to defaults even though their data survived in the .bak.
recommendation: Route all three writers through JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic (CsvManager needs a small text-file twin of it, or generalize the utility to take raw content). In ConfigurationService.Load's catch block, before falling back to defaults, attempt to parse config.json.bak and restore from it (still setting ConfigLoadError to tell the user what happened). This collapses two persistence disciplines into one and wires up the recovery asset that is already being paid for on every save.
user_benefit: A crash during save can currently wipe the user's entire preset library, environments, and host inventory back to factory defaults despite an intact backup existing on disk. One consistent write path plus .bak restore makes that whole failure class disappear.

title: Transient per-run RunningState is persisted by rewriting all of jobs.json through Save(), unsynchronized and non-atomically
existing_state: Every job run rewrites the entire jobs definitions file two to three times via the same code path users' edits go through. TryStartJob sets job.RunningState and calls _jobStorage.Save(job) (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:768-774), CompleteJob clears it and calls Save again (JobExecutionService.cs:827-832), and HandlePostExecution can call Save a third time for one-time jobs (JobExecutionService.cs:877-888). JobStorageService.Save (Services/JobStorageService.cs:113-139) is the definition-editing path: it stamps job.ModifiedUtc = DateTime.UtcNow (line 134) — so every scheduled run silently overwrites the user's real last-modified timestamp — raises JobsChanged (line 138) — triggering full UI refreshes — and calls PersistToDisk (lines 227-244), which copies jobs.json over jobs.json.bak (line 232, so the backup is rotated to a mid-run snapshot seconds after any user edit) and then writes with plain File.WriteAllText (line 243). There is no lock anywhere in JobStorageService: with MaxConcurrentJobs (default 3) plus unbounded Run Now executions (JobExecutionService.cs:236, no semaphore), two ThreadPool threads can be inside PersistToDisk at once — File.WriteAllText then throws a sharing violation, which propagates out of TryStartJob/CompleteJob and silently kills that run's start or leaves a stale RunningState (falsely reported as 'Application crashed during execution' at next startup, JobExecutionService.cs:153-168). The non-atomic write also violates the project's own JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic convention (Utilities/JsonFileWriter.cs:21), which the sibling JobHistoryService follows at every write site (Services/JobHistoryService.cs:227, 280, 425, 472, 597). A crash mid-write truncates jobs.json; Load then backs it up to .corrupt and starts with an EMPTY job list (JobStorageService.cs:89-98).
recommendation: Separate runtime state from the definition store. (1) Stop routing RunningState through Save(): add an internal PersistRunningState(jobId) path (or a small sidecar file like running-state.json keyed by job ID) that does not stamp ModifiedUtc and does not raise JobsChanged; crash recovery in Initialize() reads the sidecar instead. (2) In JobStorageService, serialize all writes behind a private lock object and replace File.WriteAllText with JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic(path, json, createBackup: true) — this also removes the hand-rolled .bak copy. (3) Only rotate .bak on definition-changing saves so the backup keeps its value as an undo point for user edits.
user_benefit: Your jobs file — the single store for every scheduled job — stops being rewritten dozens of times an hour by the scheduler itself, can no longer be truncated by a crash or clobbered by two concurrent runs, and 'last modified' starts meaning when you actually edited the job.

title: SchedulingService has no canonical timezone semantics — UI previews use local-time cron interpretation while the execution engine fires in UTC
existing_state: The same service exposes two incompatible interpretations of the same cron expression and callers picked different ones. GetNextRunLocal (Services/SchedulingService.cs:53-63) passes TimeZoneInfo.Local to Cronos, so cron fields mean local wall-clock time; GetMissedOccurrences (SchedulingService.cs:89-100) uses the zone-less Cronos overload, so the same fields mean UTC. Every user-facing surface uses the local interpretation: the Job List 'Next Run' column (JobListDialog.cs:741), the main-form status-bar countdown (Form1.cs:15230), and the cron builder's live preview in the job editor (UI/CronBuilderControl.cs:622). But the actual due-check that fires jobs uses the UTC interpretation (JobExecutionService.IsJobDue, Services/JobExecutionService.cs:1028 → GetMissedOccurrences), as does startup missed-run detection (SchedulingService.cs:126, 165). On any machine not running UTC, a job built as 'Daily at 9:00 AM' previews 9:00 AM local in three places and then fires at 9:00 AM UTC — hours off. The structure (parallel Local/Utc methods with no designated source of truth, callers choosing ad hoc) is what bred the defect, and nothing prevents the next caller from picking the wrong one again.
recommendation: Make one interpretation canonical and funnel all occurrence math through it. Decide that cron fields mean local wall-clock time (what every preview already promises users), change GetMissedOccurrences to call cron.GetOccurrences with TimeZoneInfo.Local (Cronos supports a zone-aware overload), and delete or internalize GetNextRunUtc so there is a single occurrence API the executor, missed-run detector, and all UI surfaces share. Add a regression test asserting next-run preview and IsJobDue agree on a non-UTC TimeZoneInfo.
user_benefit: Scheduled jobs run at the time the UI told you they would. Today every preview lies by your UTC offset, which for a fleet-automation tool means commands hitting production hosts at the wrong hour.

title: Two expression engines disagree on truthiness, comparison, and equality — same expression, different answer in if: vs set:
existing_state: Conditions (if/elif/while/when/assert) run through ExpressionEvaluator; set: right-hand sides and ternaries run through ExpressionParser — and their semantics have already diverged in three ways. (1) Truthiness of "0": ExpressionParser.IsTruthy treats the string "0" as false (Services/Scripting/ExpressionParser.cs:163-173), while the evaluator's bare-value fallback uses ValueResolver.IsTruthyValue (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:205-207), where "0" is truthy (ValueResolver.cs:347-359; the structured-emptiness helper at 497-509 only applies to '{'/'[' strings). So `if x` is TRUE but `set: y = x ? "a" : "b"` picks "b" for the same x="0". (2) `>`/`<`: the evaluator coerces non-numeric operands to 0 (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:368-376), the parser falls back to case-insensitive STRING comparison (ExpressionParser.cs:152-161). (3) `==`: the evaluator compares numerics with a 0.0001 epsilon (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:399-416), the parser uses exact double CompareTo (ExpressionParser.cs:140-150). Which engine answers is decided by a syntax sniff — ExpressionEvaluator.ResolveValue re-routes into ExpressionParser only when the text "looks computable" (contains '(', '?', ' + ', etc., ExpressionEvaluator.cs:320-360) and swallows all parse exceptions — so adding parentheses or a '+' to a condition silently changes its comparison semantics.
recommendation: Make ValueResolver the single source of truth for scalar semantics (it already is for emptiness/collections per its design): extract shared CompareValues/CompareNumeric/AreEqual/IsTruthy primitives into ValueResolver and have BOTH ExpressionEvaluator and ExpressionParser delegate to them, picking one documented rule per operator (suggested: parser's numeric-then-string ordering for >/<, one equality rule, one truthiness table). This kills the three divergences without a rewrite. A later phase can fold condition parsing into the ExpressionParser grammar (add and/or/not/in/matches) so there is one engine, but the primitive extraction alone removes the user-facing inconsistency.
user_benefit: Eliminates the worst class of silent wrong-result bugs in fleet scripts: a condition that works in `if:` behaving differently inside a ternary or after a cosmetic edit, branching wrongly across hundreds of hosts with no error shown.

title: Function dispatch is split across three unsynchronized layers — the most-used built-ins bypass the registry, creating a silent-shadowing trap and blocking function tooling
existing_state: The ~112-name callable function surface is dispatched through three independent layers. (1) FunctionRegistry registers 8 category classes = 71 functions (Services/Scripting/FunctionRegistry.cs:92-102) and is the only enumerable layer (Count/RegisteredNames, FunctionRegistry.cs:85-90). (2) Twenty legacy functions — including the most-used ones: length, trim, upper, lower, replace, split, join, sort, first, last, indexof, concat, substring — live in a hardcoded switch in JsonUtilities.TryEvaluateFunctionExpression (Services/Scripting/JsonUtilities.cs:347-564), reached only after a registry miss (JsonUtilities.cs:343-345); StringFunctions registers contains/startswith/pad/regex_*/format/uuid etc. but NOT those core names, so they live permanently outside the Functions/ category architecture CLAUDE.md guideline 3 designates for built-ins. (3) The json.* family is a third hardcoded switch (JsonUtilities.cs:679-770). Concrete consequences verified: (a) because the registry is consulted FIRST and Register() silently overwrites duplicates (FunctionRegistry.cs:37-43), registering any new function whose name collides with a legacy one (e.g. adding 'replace' to StringFunctions with the library's usual ignore-case semantics, while legacy replace is case-SENSITIVE Ordinal at JsonUtilities.cs:394, vs the OrdinalIgnoreCase string operators in conditions at ExpressionEvaluator.cs:124-148) silently changes the behavior of every existing script — no error, no warning; (b) unknown-function behavior is inconsistent by call position: in condition context ExpressionParser.ResolveFunction throws FormatException 'Unknown function' (Services/Scripting/ExpressionParser.cs:422-436), but in value context ResolveJsonValue silently falls through to variable lookup and finally returns the typo as a literal string (JsonUtilities.cs:307-333), so `set: x = uper(host)` assigns the text 'uper(host)'. Finally, Services/Editor/ScriptAutocompleteProvider.cs contains zero references to FunctionRegistry or any function name (verified by grep), so the editor offers no completion for any of the ~112 functions — and it cannot be built correctly today because RegisteredNames under-reports the surface by ~40%.
recommendation: Consolidate to one dispatch table. Port the 20 legacy switch cases into a category class registered in FunctionRegistry.RegisterBuiltInCategories (behavior-preserving — keep replace case-sensitive unless explicitly decided otherwise); route json.* through the registry as dotted names (TryParseFunctionCall already accepts '.' in names, JsonUtilities.cs:584), reducing TryEvaluateFunctionExpression to registry-only dispatch. Make Register throw (or Debug.Assert) on duplicate names to convert the silent-shadowing trap into a build-time failure. Then make ResolveJsonValue's fall-through explicit: if TryParseFunctionCall succeeds but the name is unknown, emit a script warning instead of resolving the call text as a literal. This unblocks editor autocomplete and parser-time function-name validation as follow-ups.
user_benefit: Eliminates a trap where adding any new built-in can silently change the meaning of existing fleet scripts, makes function typos visible instead of producing literal garbage values, and unblocks editor autocomplete/validation for the whole function surface.

title: Host credential resolution is forked between Form1 and JobExecutionService and has already diverged
existing_state: The contract 'turn host rows into HostConnections with credentials' is implemented twice in full: Form1.GetHostConnections (Form1.cs:13301-13389) for interactive runs and JobExecutionService.BuildHostConnections (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:487-544) for scheduled jobs. Both re-implement host parsing, explicit-port-beats-port-column precedence (the TryGetExplicitPortFromHostValue helper is copy-pasted as a private static at JobExecutionService.cs:564-587), vault_path-first resolution, and the username/password column fallback. They have already drifted in a way that produces wrong results: the grid path silently auto-saves any typed password to Windows Credential Manager and auto-loads the stored per-host password when the cell is empty (Form1.cs:13345-13357), while the job path has no Credential Manager per-host lookup at all — a job in PerHostColumn mode (ResolveCredentials returns ("","") for that mode, JobExecutionService.cs:624-626) whose rows have empty password cells connects with an empty password and fails at schedule time, even though the identical rows work in the grid. Every job-side failure path is a Debug.WriteLine plus empty strings (JobExecutionService.cs:605, 620, 639), so the divergence surfaces only as 2am authentication failures.
recommendation: Extract a single HostCredentialResolver service (rows -> List<HostConnection>) consumed by both Form1 and JobExecutionService, with the Credential Manager per-host fallback policy made explicit and shared (or explicitly opted out for jobs, in one documented place). Move the duplicated port/host parsing helpers into it. This is also the natural seam for making resolution awaitable, parallel, and properly error-surfaced instead of two.
user_benefit: Hosts that authenticate fine in the grid stop mysteriously failing when the same rows run as a scheduled job, and future changes to credential precedence only need to be made (and tested) once instead of being silently missed on one of the two paths.

title: Vault and Notification profile managers are copy-paste twins that have already drifted into live defects
existing_state: SettingsDialog.cs contains two parallel hand-rolled implementations of the same list+detail+credential-store profile manager (Vault ~lines 742-1178, Notifications ~1342-1693), and they have diverged in ways that are each a defect: (1) Rename — notifications migrate Credential Manager secrets old->new then delete the old target (1557-1564, MigrateNotificationCredential 1584-1593); Vault rename (997-1005) just relabels the list and re-saves secrets under the new name (1011-1017), permanently orphaning live ssh_helper:vault:<oldname>:* secrets in Windows Credential Manager. (2) Enum mapping — Vault uses raw (VaultKvVersion)/(VaultAuthMethod) SelectedIndex casts (981-982) while notifications use explicit switches (1374-1394) that omit NotificationChannelKind.Toast = 3 (Models/NotificationSettings.cs:95): a Toast-kind profile loads as Slack and 'profile.Kind = GetSelectedNotificationKind()' (1548) silently rewrites it to Slack on the next selection change. (3) Add — BtnVaultAdd_Click flushes pending edits first (820); BtnNotificationAdd_Click (1424-1440) does not and suppresses the selection-change persist (1429-1432), silently dropping unsaved edits to the previously selected notification profile. (4) Default profile — Vault uncheck is a no-op (early return at 808) while notifications support clearing (1418-1421). Make both tabs thin adapters over it. While extracting, fix the three live defects: add Vault rename migration mirroring MigrateNotificationCredential, add the Toast=3 arm (or guard unknown kinds from being persisted), and flush pending edits in BtnNotificationAdd_Click.
user_benefit: Stops the slow corruption this duplication is already causing — orphaned secrets accumulating in Credential Manager after renames, notification profiles silently changing kind, and edits vanishing on Add — and makes the next profile-type tab (or field) a one-place change.

title: No staging layer: dialogs mutate Credential Manager and disk during navigation, making Cancel structurally impossible
existing_state: SettingsDialog presents itself as staged-until-Save (everything funnels through one _configService.Update in BtnSave_Click, SettingsDialog.cs:2657-2755), but secrets bypass the staging entirely: PersistVaultProfileByIndex runs on every profile selection change (795) and writes or deletes Credential Manager entries right then (1011-1017; SaveVaultCredential 1020-1027 deletes the credential when the textbox is empty). Notifications do the same (1401, 1577-1581, 1595-1602). The Remove buttons purge stored secrets immediately (Vault 851-858, Notifications 1450-1455). Net effect: clicking Remove then Cancel leaves config.json still referencing a profile whose secrets are irreversibly gone; renaming then cancelling leaves credentials migrated/duplicated for a rename that never happened. EnvironmentDialog has the same architecture: every action (New 427, Duplicate, Rename, Delete, Import) and every selection change (408) persists straight to disk through EnvironmentService, and the Save button's only real effect is setting SelectedEnvironmentName (639-643) — Cancel is cosmetic, and the persist path swallows all exceptions (819-822). This single structural decision is the root of the whole cancel-doesn't-cancel defect family the dialogs exhibit, and every new profile field added inherits the same pre-Save-mutation trap.
recommendation: Introduce per-dialog staged state for external side effects: hold pending secret values in an in-memory map (profile -> slot -> value, with a tombstone for deletions), populate textboxes from it, and flush to Credential Manager only inside BtnSave_Click after ValidateVaultProfiles passes; queue Remove's credential purges the same way. For EnvironmentDialog, operate on a cloned environment map (LoadEnvironmentState already returns clones) and commit through EnvironmentService once on Save. Immediate-action buttons that must stay immediate (Clear Browser Data, Reset Preset Timeouts) should be visually marked as such.
user_benefit: Cancel actually cancels: no more losing stored Vault tokens or webhook URLs from a dialog session the user backed out of, and no orphaned config-to-credential references that fail mysteriously at run time.

title: Lambda parameters are bound by mutating the shared ScriptContext — collection functions produce wrong results under parallel:
existing_state: LambdaExpression.Evaluate implements lambda parameters (map/filter/reduce/find/any/all/count) by writing the parameter into the script's global variable table via context.SetVariable, evaluating the body, then restoring the saved value (Services/Scripting/LambdaExpression.cs:60-90). There is no scoped evaluation environment — the single shared Dictionary<string,object?> in ScriptContext (Services/Scripting/ScriptContext.cs:99, 513) is the only binding mechanism; its per-operation locks (ScriptContext.cs:528-599) prevent dictionary corruption but not logical races. ParallelCommand runs child steps concurrently on the SAME context — the comment at Services/Scripting/Commands/ParallelCommand.cs:45 says 'Steps share one context; script context/session enforce internal synchronization' (Task.Run per step at :40-50). So two parallel branches that each evaluate a lambda using the same parameter name (the idiomatic `x`) interleave SetVariable('x', ...) calls: branch A's body can read branch B's element mid-iteration, and the save/restore in the finally block can resurrect or delete the wrong value. Results are intermittently wrong with no error. The same mechanism also means a lambda parameter silently shadows any same-named script/CSV variable for the duration of each element evaluation — on a single thread that is restored correctly, but it is the structural reason the parallel case cannot be fixed locally.
recommendation: Introduce a scoped variable overlay instead of mutating shared state: give ExpressionParser (and ValueResolver lookups it performs) an optional overlay dictionary checked before context.GetVariable, and have LambdaExpression.Evaluate pass {param: value} as that overlay (Services/Scripting/LambdaExpression.cs:74-78 already constructs the parser per call, so threading an overlay through is contained). Alternatively, have ParallelCommand hand each branch a child context that copy-on-writes variables — but the overlay is smaller and also fixes lambdas invoked from any future concurrent path. Add a regression test: parallel: with two foreach+map branches over distinct lists using parameter `x`, assert per-branch results.
user_benefit: Scripts that combine two advertised features — parallel: blocks and collection lambdas — currently can compute intermittently wrong values (e.g. wrong host lists) with zero diagnostics; this makes the combination safe.

title: No global exception handling: any unhandled error kills the app with no log and no state flush
existing_state: Program.Main (Program.cs:13-60) calls Application.Run(new Form1()) at Program.cs:59 with no try/catch, and a repo-wide search for Application.ThreadException, AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException, TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException, and SetUnhandledExceptionMode returns zero hits in any .cs file. The shell is a 15,360-line Form1.cs plus async void handlers (e.g. Form1_Shown at Form1.cs:414) wired to an SSH engine, a cron scheduler, and WebView2 bridges. Today any stray exception on the UI thread shows the stock .NET crash dialog, and one on a worker/Task thread silently terminates the process — unsaved host-grid edits (_csvDirty state), running executions, and the active scheduler all die with zero diagnostics written anywhere. ScintillaNativeBootstrap.ConfigureSatelliteDirectory (Program.cs:58) can itself throw InvalidOperationException pre-UI (ScintillaNativeBootstrap.cs:84-86) and is equally unhandled.
recommendation: In Program.Main, before Application.Run: call Application.SetUnhandledExceptionMode(UnhandledExceptionMode.CatchException), subscribe Application.ThreadException, AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException, and TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException. The shared handler should append exception + stack to a crash log under AppDataPaths.GetAppFolder() (e.g. crash.log), show a themed 'unexpected error' dialog with the log path, and on fatal paths attempt a best-effort SaveApplicationState/config flush before exit. Also wrap the ConfigureSatelliteDirectory call so a Scintilla extraction failure produces a message instead of a pre-UI hard crash.
user_benefit: Bugs stop costing users their unsaved fleet edits and their scheduler session, and every crash leaves a log you can actually debug from instead of a one-off 'it just closed' report.

title: Graph structure has two competing sources of truth (edges vs _isChildOf/_stepPath metadata) with no central normalization seam
existing_state: Container membership is decided by node metadata (_isChildOf + _stepPath), NOT edges, for imported graphs -- but canvas-built graphs have no metadata, so every structural consumer carries a dual-origin code path: treeBuilder tries buildBranchesMeta then falls back to buildBranchesEdges (FlowCanvas/src/utils/layout/treeBuilder.ts:63-67); edgePath classifies branch edges via data.branchPath OR target _isChildOf and correlates taken-branches two different ways (edgePath.ts:58-63, 177-192); branchBands groups purely by _isChildOf (branchBands.ts:156-169); export regeneration rebuilds nesting from metadata. childMembership.ts:1-12 documents the seam and exists precisely because wiring a fresh block used to orphan it. This duplication has a documented defect history (issue #45 sibling drop/promote, the rewire-into-band bug, the _stepPath-contiguity dead-neon bug), and a live hole remains today: pasteNodes deep-copies node data verbatim (utils/clipboard.ts:44-57) and the paste site strips nothing (hooks/useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:63-74), so a pasted child still carries _isChildOf/_stepPath pointing at the ORIGINAL container -- branchBands draws it inside the original band, treeBuilder nests it under the original container, renumberStepPaths renumbers it as a sibling of the original branch, and metadata-driven export can double-place it. Every new structural entry point (paste today; future duplicate/drag-into-band/group ops) must independently remember all metadata invariants or it ships another bug of this class.
recommendation: Introduce a single normalization seam: a normalizeStructure(nodes, edges) pass owning the invariants (membership matches wiring, _stepPath contiguous per branch, cosmetics/_forceGraphExport consistent) that every structural entry point routes through -- import (load-graph), onConnect, paste, delete paths, undo/redo restore. Short-term, fix paste inside it (strip or remap _isChildOf/_stepPath/_membershipFromConnect via the paste idMap). Longer-term, collapse the dual origin: derive and write membership metadata for canvas-authored nodes at connect time for ALL gestures (childMembership already covers three), so treeBuilder/edgePath/branchBands can drop their edge-walking fallbacks and metadata becomes the only structural source of truth.
user_benefit: Stops the recurring class of wrong-band / wrong-export / dead-highlight bugs that has already produced several shipped defects, and makes new graph operations (duplicate, group, drag-into-container) safe to build.

title: Release pipeline has zero test gates: dotnet test and the vitest suite never run, and push/PR CI is disabled
existing_state: The only workflow is build-release.yml, triggered solely by `v*` tags and manual dispatch — the `branches: ["master"]` push trigger and the entire pull_request trigger are commented out (build-release.yml:5, 8-9). No workflow anywhere runs `dotnet test`, so the whole SSH_Helper.Tests xUnit suite (including the ScriptSamples validation suite and the FlowCanvasBridge parity tests that the project leans on heavily) never executes in CI. The FlowCanvas vitest unit suite (`npm test`) also never runs. The single gate that does exist is the heaviest, most environment-sensitive layer: the full Playwright e2e suite (line 43) chained via `needs: flowcanvas-browser-tests` (line 56) in front of the release build — meaning known-flaky e2e specs can block a tagged release while fast deterministic regressions sail onto master completely unchecked.
recommendation: Add a CI job (or separate ci.yml) that runs on push/PR to master: `dotnet test SSH_Helper.Tests/SSH_Helper.Tests.csproj -p:SkipFlowCanvasBuild=true` (windows runner) and `npm test` in FlowCanvas/ (ubuntu runner) — both are minutes, not the e2e half-hour. In build-release.yml, make the release `build` job `need` these fast suites; keep the full Playwright run as a parallel signal or a tag-only gate depending on its current stability. Re-enable the commented push/PR triggers.
user_benefit: Regressions get caught at commit time instead of at release-tag time (or in users' hands). Right now the most valuable test assets in the repo are invisible to the pipeline that ships binaries.

title: Two divergent CSV parsers: job host import silently corrupts CSVs the app itself wrote
existing_state: CsvManager contains two independent CSV parsers. The grid load path uses ReadCsvRecord (CsvManager.cs:118-189), a full record reader that supports quoted fields with embedded newlines — and the app's own save path deliberately produces such fields: EscapeCsvValue quotes any value containing \n or \r (CsvManager.cs:254-256). The second parser, public static ParseCsvLine (CsvManager.cs:194-243), is line-based and cannot handle embedded newlines. JobStorageService.ImportHostsFromCsv uses the second one: it does File.ReadAllLines and parses each physical line independently (JobStorageService.cs:263-285, delegating at 311-312). Result: a hosts CSV exported by the app's own Save (or any RFC-compliant CSV) containing a multi-line cell loads perfectly into the main grid but, when imported into a scheduled job, splits the quoted record across lines — the first fragment becomes a short row and the continuation line becomes a bogus extra 'host' — with no error. The job then targets a corrupted host list.
recommendation: Delete the duplication: expose the record-based reader (ReadCsvRecord, or a LoadFromFile overload returning rows) as the single parsing entry point and rewrite JobStorageService.ImportHostsFromCsv to stream records through it instead of File.ReadAllLines + ParseCsvLine. Keep ParseCsvLine only if a genuinely single-line use case remains, and document it as such.
user_benefit: Job host imports stop silently diverging from grid imports for the same file — no phantom hosts or truncated rows in scheduled jobs, and one parser to fix when the next CSV edge case shows up.

evidence.note: Record reader handles embedded newlines; ParseCsvLine does not; EscapeCsvValue emits quoted newlines on save
ImportHostsFromCsv: File.ReadAllLines + per-line ParseCsvLine — breaks on quoted multi-line fields

title: on_error handling has no single enforcement point — continue-paths in readfile/writefile return plain Ok, which erases _last_error and hides the error from the canvas
existing_state: CommandResult.ApplyOnError (Services/Scripting/Commands/IScriptCommand.cs:136-141) is the intended single mapping: on_error:continue -> Suppressed (sets SuppressedError=true). But each command hand-rolls the check, and several diverge. ReadFileCommand returns plain CommandResult.Ok(message) on continue for extension-config errors (ReadFileCommand.cs:62-63), extension-mismatch (84-85), blocked-path validation (95-96), and missing file (113-114). WriteFileCommand does the same for path-validation (WriteFileCommand.cs:54-61) yet correctly returns Suppressed for IO exceptions in the very same file (148-149, 158-159). PlaySoundCommand silently defaults to continue when on_error is omitted — unique among all commands (PlaySoundCommand.cs:127-134). Notify and Vault honor a second, options-level on_error in addition to the step-level one (NotifyCommand.cs:89). The consequence is concrete: ScriptExecutor sets _last_error only when SuppressedError is true and actively REMOVES _last_error on a plain-Ok success (ScriptExecutor.cs:412-419), so a continued readfile/writefile validation failure both fails to record its error AND erases any prior error trail a script was inspecting. SuppressedError also flows onto StepCompleted events (ScriptExecutor.cs:408) and into the Flow Canvas step payload (Form1.cs:13647), so these steps render as clean successes in the canvas instead of suppressed-error state.
recommendation: Make CommandResult.ApplyOnError the only continue/stop mapping: replace every `if (IsContinueOnError(step)) return CommandResult.Ok(...)` site in ReadFileCommand and WriteFileCommand with `return CommandResult.ApplyOnError(step, msg)` (or Suppressed directly), and delete the per-command IsContinueOnError helpers (WriteFileCommand.cs:165-168 duplicates step.IsOnErrorContinue). Decide whether playsound's default-continue is intended; if yes, express it via a declarative flag on the command registration (e.g., DefaultOnErrorContinue) rather than a buried private method, so the contract is discoverable. Add one unit test per command asserting SuppressedError=true on continued failures — the existing test suite already asserts this pattern for other commands, so the gap is cheap to close.
user_benefit: Scripts that use on_error: continue plus ${_last_error} checks (the documented error-handling pattern) get correct results from readfile/writefile, and the Flow Canvas stops showing real (suppressed) failures as green successes.

title: set's expression dispatch is a five-layer heuristic gate whose patch-guards are fossils of past misparse bugs — and it still silently turns literals like 2024-1 into arithmetic
existing_state: SetCommand.EvaluateExpression (Services/Scripting/Commands/SetCommand.cs:97-198) routes each assignment through an ordered chain: string-prefix-matched push/unshift/pop/shift (101-176), built-in function expressions, JSON expressions, then ExpressionParser — but only when HasExpressionOperator fires (184-195). That gate is pure heuristics: '+'/'-' count as operators only when preceded by whitespace, a guard added so hyphenated hostnames like db-master.local are not subtracted (245-248); a separate IsSimpleCompactNumericBinaryExpression special case re-admits compact numerics (266-306) with its own HasAmbiguousLeadingZero guard so 2024-01 stays a string (300-302, 308-318). Each guard is a patch over an earlier silent misparse, and holes remain: `set: v = 2024-1` passes the compact check (no leading zero on either operand) and evaluates to 2023; `set: v = 1.2-3` becomes -1.8 — both silently, with only a Debug-level echo (39). Meanwhile if/while conditions always evaluate through ExpressionEvaluator (which delegates to the same ExpressionParser, ExpressionEvaluator.cs:333), so the identical text is an expression in `if:` but maybe-a-string in `set:` depending on spacing — behavior nobody can predict without reading this method. The dead ResolveValue pass-through wrapper (320-323) and a comment referencing the already-deleted ArithmeticParser (391) show the layer has been reworked repeatedly.
recommendation: Replace the guess-the-intent gate with an explicit rule and one downgrade path: treat the right-hand side as an expression whenever ExpressionParser can fully consume it AND it contains an unambiguous operator token (operator with surrounding whitespace, or parentheses); otherwise treat it as a literal/substitution — deleting IsSimpleCompactNumericBinaryExpression and its leading-zero guard outright (compact `1+2` users can write `1 + 2`). Document the rule in the script reference, and emit an Info-level (not Debug) line whenever an assignment was evaluated as arithmetic so misparses are visible in normal output. Add regression tests for the fossil cases: hyphenated hostnames, 2024-01, 2024-1, 1.2-3.
user_benefit: Assignments stop silently changing meaning based on invisible spacing rules, and the next hostname-like or version-like literal will not require yet another guard patch shipped after a user hits data corruption in their variables.

title: Job save is split across two dialogs and persists the Credential Manager secret before the job itself, with no rollback
existing_state: Saving a job is a two-form transaction with the steps in the wrong order. JobEditorDialog.ValidateAndSave writes the stored credential to Windows Credential Manager first (JobEditorDialog.cs:2060-2064 -> TryPersistStoredCredentials :1964-2010, keyed by CredentialTargets.JobPasswordTarget(_editingJob.Id)), then merely returns the edited JobDefinition via Result (:2135-2137). The actual job persistence happens later in the CALLER: JobListDialog.OnNewClick (:1041-1052) and EditSelectedJob (:1354-1365) call _jobStorage.Save inside a try/catch that just shows a 'Failed to save job' message box. If Save throws, a New job leaves an orphaned secret in CredMan for a job id that never existed, and an Edit leaves a rotated password attached to the OLD job definition — the next scheduled run silently uses the new password with stale settings (or the user believes the rotation failed entirely and retries differently). The team has already hit this bug class once: the Duplicate path got the correct ordering with rollback (SaveDuplicatedJob, JobListDialog.cs:1295-1308 saves the job first, then copies the credential, and deletes the job on credential failure) — but the fix was applied only there, not to New/Edit, precisely because the save responsibility is scattered across two forms.
recommendation: Centralize the job+secret save in one place with the same ordering Duplicate already uses: have JobEditorDialog stop writing to CredMan and instead expose the pending username/password (e.g., a PendingStoredCredential on the dialog alongside Result); JobListDialog (or a small JobSaveCoordinator service) then does _jobStorage.Save first, persists the secret second, and rolls the job back (or surfaces a precise partial-failure message) if the secret write fails — mirroring SaveDuplicatedJob:1295-1308.
user_benefit: Job definitions and their stored passwords can no longer get out of sync on a failed save, preventing orphaned secrets in Credential Manager and scheduled runs that silently authenticate with mismatched credentials after a partial failure.

title: Breakpoints/disabled/expanded live in three places at once (slice Sets + node.data flags + host) with no single source of truth
existing_state: Block view-state is triple-represented: `debugSlice` keeps `breakpoints`/`disabledBlocks`/`expandedNodes` Sets, every toggle also mirrors a flag into node.data (`breakpoint`, `execState:'disabled'`, `expanded`) and notifies the C# host (stores/slices/debugSlice.ts:41-108). The copies already desynchronize through two concrete mechanisms: (1) `load-graph` restores the disabled and expanded Sets from node.data but never clears or restores `breakpoints` (stores/messageBridge.ts:162-183), and `resetGraphSessionState` doesn't touch them either (messageBridge.ts:74-81) — since preset node ids collide (`node-1`, `node-2`, …), switching presets in an open canvas silently carries the previous preset's breakpoints onto unrelated blocks of the next one (a known-but-unfixed leak; the disabled/expanded half of this exact bug class was already fixed once). (2) Undo/redo restores `nodes`/`edges` only (stores/slices/undoSlice.ts:30-98), so undoing past a breakpoint or expand toggle restores `data.breakpoint`/`data.expanded` while the Sets — which drive the gutter dot via `hasBreakpoint`, layout height estimation via `isExpanded`, and host notifications — keep the newer values: visuals, layout, and the C# executor's breakpoint list now disagree.
recommendation: Pick node.data as the single source: derive `hasBreakpoint`/`isDisabled`/`isExpanded` from node.data via selectors, delete the Sets, and recompute+resend the host's breakpoint list whenever nodes are replaced wholesale (load-graph, undo, redo). Short of the full refactor, the two-line mitigations are: clear `breakpoints` in `resetGraphSessionState` (re-notifying the host per removed id), and re-derive all three Sets from node.data after every undo/redo.
user_benefit: Eliminates a whole class of 'the canvas and the debugger disagree' bugs: phantom breakpoints pausing the wrong preset's blocks, gutter dots that don't match what the executor will actually stop on, and expanded-vs-layout overlap after undo.

title: Vault credential-slot names are a three-file implicit contract; the authType parameter is decorative and disagrees with reality
existing_state: VaultService passes "token"/"approle"/"ldap"/"userpass" as the second argument to its credential providers (Services/Vault/VaultService.cs:317, 329, 370, 408, 884), but every production provider discards that argument: Form1's lambdas bind it to _ and hardcode the different literals "token"/"approle_secret"/"ldap_password"/"userpass_password" (Form1.cs:1396-1415), and SettingsDialog independently hardcodes the same four strings when persisting secrets (SettingsDialog.cs:1013-1016) and ignores the parameter again in its Test Connection providers (SettingsDialog.cs:1062-1066). The system works only because two UI files agree by copy-paste convention; any future caller that trusts the parameter VaultService actually sends (e.g. "approle") reads or writes a credential slot that nothing else uses. Compounding it, Token auth and the OIDC persisted-token fast path share the same ":token" slot (read at VaultService.cs:317 and :884, written by the tokenSaver at Form1.cs:1416-1420), so toggling a profile between Token and OIDC auth silently overwrites the user's static token with short-lived OIDC tokens.
recommendation: Promote the four authType literals to constants on CredentialTargets (already the declared single source of truth for target names in Services/Credentials/CredentialTargets.cs), make VaultService pass those constants, and change the Form1/SettingsDialog provider lambdas to use the parameter instead of ignoring it — deleting the duplicate literals. Give OIDC its own slot constant (e.g. "oidc_token") with a one-time fallback read of the legacy "token" slot so existing logins survive.
user_benefit: Eliminates a latent wrong-credential-slot trap that will bite the next feature touching Vault auth (the compiler will enforce the contract instead of copy-paste), and stops OIDC logins from clobbering a user's stored static Vault token.

title: Application version has no single source of truth: hardcoded const drives updates while the assembly says 1.0.0.0
existing_state: The real version exists only as private const ApplicationVersion = "0.51.23" in Form1.cs:115. SSH_Helper.csproj contains no <Version>/<AssemblyVersion>/<FileVersion> property at all (verified — the only Version strings are PackageReference attributes), so the compiled exe's assembly/file version is the default 1.0.0.0 and disagrees with the title bar (Form1.cs:329). Critically, UpdateService is constructed with this const (Form1.cs:374-377) and compares GitHub releases against it — so each release requires manually bumping the const, the git branch name (currently also '0.51.23'), and the GitHub tag in sync. A missed const bump means every user is re-offered the version they already run (update loop) or never offered the next one; meanwhile file-properties/installer tooling sees 1.0.0.0 forever.
recommendation: Add <Version>0.51.23</Version> to SSH_Helper.csproj as the single source (CI can override via -p:Version=). Replace the const with a static property reading Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().GetCustomAttribute<AssemblyInformationalVersionAttribute>() (trimming any +commit suffix) and use it for the title, AboutDialog, NoUpdateDialog, and the UpdateService comparison. Delete the Form1.cs:115 const.
user_benefit: Releases can no longer ship with a stale in-app version that breaks the self-updater for every user, and the exe's file properties finally match the product version.

title: Three near-identical script execution backends inside SshExecutionService with visible behavioral drift
existing_state: ExecuteScriptWithPool (Services/SshExecutionService.cs:1501-1572), ExecuteScriptWithoutPool (:1578-1703), and ExecuteScriptLocal (:1705-1759) each independently re-implement the same sequence: header banner build, ScriptContext creation, ConfigureScriptExecutionContext, AttachScriptExecutionEventHandlers, ScriptExecutor construction + the three debug-event re-subscriptions, EnsureScriptSucceeded. The duplication has already produced divergence: (1) header format differs for the same feature — pooled emits "# {host} {prompt} SCRIPT: {name} #" (:1531) while non-pooled emits "# SCRIPT: {host} {prompt}{name} #" (:1665), so transcripts/history for identical runs differ by pooling setting; (2) session.DebugOutput is subscribed only in the non-pooled path (:1637-1643) — pooled script runs silently drop all session-level debug output (prompt detection, banner handling), even though the simple-command pooled path does subscribe it (:2115-2119); (3) post-init FlushBuffer is called only in the non-pooled simple path (:2270) — both script paths and the pooled simple path skip it, so residual login-banner data can bleed into the first command's output on those paths only. These are inside a 2,897-line service, so each new script feature (relay state, preconnect, Flow Canvas debug bootstrap) had to be threaded through all three copies.
recommendation: Collapse the trio into one RunScriptCore(host, script, sessionProvider, ...) where the only varying piece is a small session acquisition strategy (pooled lease / direct connect / null for local) and the header prefix string. The shared body owns header emission, context configuration, event wiring (including session.DebugOutput uniformly), executor execution, and cleanup. Fix the header format and DebugOutput drift in the process — one format, one subscription policy.
user_benefit: Identical script runs produce identical transcripts and identical debug diagnostics regardless of the pooling toggle, and future script-engine features get wired once instead of three times (the class's history shows each copy is a place to forget).

title: Connect/login/algorithm-fallback ladder is fully duplicated between SshExecutionService and SshConnectionPool — and has already drifted
existing_state: The entire connection pipeline exists twice. Service side: CreateConnectedClientWithFallback (Services/SshExecutionService.cs:2372-2493), ApplyAlgorithmTier (:2499-2514), ShouldRetryWithAlgorithmFallback/HasUnsupportedKeyAlgorithmError/TrySetSshParameterAlgorithms (:2516-2555), plus the agent→identity-file→password login order written out twice more (:1602-1614, :2199-2213). Pool side: CreateConnectionAsync (Services/SshConnectionPool.cs:365-459), LoginClient (:461-475), ApplyAlgorithmTier (:477-490), HasUnsupportedKeyAlgorithmError (:492-500), TrySetMacAlgorithms (:502-506), ApplyAlgorithmSettings (:512+). Verified drift between the copies today: (1) the service's HasUnsupportedKeyAlgorithmError has a CryptographicException-typed branch (:2542-2546) the pool's lacks (:492-500); (2) the service ladder is instrumented with SshDebugLog at every step (:2381-2487) while pool CreateConnectionAsync has zero debug logging — the same connect failure is diagnosable on the direct path and opaque on the pooled path; (3) retry scope differs — the service's fallback try wraps Connect only (:2410-2419) while the pool wraps Connect+Login together (:408-418), so the two paths classify failures differently. Every cross-cutting change (e.g. adding host-key verification, which is currently absent) must be applied at 8 separate Connect() sites across the two files (service :2393, :2412, :2444, :2485; pool :389, :411, :433, :452).
recommendation: Extract a single SshClientFactory (or static SshClientConnector) owning: tier cache lookup, the three-tier connect ladder, ApplyAlgorithmSettings, the agent/key/password login order, and an optional debug-log callback. Both CreateConnectedClientWithFallback and SshConnectionPool.CreateConnectionAsync become thin wrappers over it; delete the pool's private copies of ApplyAlgorithmTier/HasUnsupportedKeyAlgorithmError/TrySetMacAlgorithms/ApplyAlgorithmSettings and the two extra in-service login blocks. This also creates the single choke point you'll need when host-key verification is added.
user_benefit: Connect behavior, fallback decisions, and diagnostics become identical whether pooling is on or off, and future SSH-layer fixes (host-key verification above all) only need to be made once instead of at 8 call sites in 2 files.

title: Four parallel implementations of 'read a Vault secret' with divergent parsing, error semantics, and cancellation behavior
existing_state: Four call sites independently re-implement profile resolution + path parsing + error policy on top of VaultService: (1) VaultCredentialProvider.ParseVaultPath for the vault_path column (Services/Vault/VaultCredentialProvider.cs:78-124); (2) hand-rolled parsing inside ScriptContext.ResolveVaultExpression for inline {{vault:...}} (Services/Scripting/ScriptContext.cs:715-744); (3) VaultCommand for the vault: step (Services/Scripting/Commands/VaultCommand.cs:22-57); (4) VaultFunctions for vault()/vault_list() (Services/Scripting/Functions/VaultFunctions.cs:16-69). The duplication has already produced user-visible inconsistency: the inline expression sets _last_error and resolves to "" (ScriptContext.cs:751-755); the step fails the run or returns Suppressed + _last_error (VaultCommand.cs:50-56); the functions swallow VaultException entirely and return null without setting anything (VaultFunctions.cs:38-41, 65-68) — so the same script cannot distinguish 'key missing' from 'Vault sealed' depending on which of the three spellings it used, and a Vault outage seen through vault() is indistinguishable from a missing key. Surfaces (1), (2) and (4) also each independently chose sync-over-async (.GetAwaiter().GetResult() at VaultCredentialProvider.cs:48-49, ScriptContext.cs:748, VaultFunctions.cs:36 and :63) and pass no CancellationToken, so a cancelled script still blocks inside an in-flight inline vault read, while (3) is properly async with cancellation (VaultCommand.cs:70).
recommendation: Extract one internal VaultAccess helper owning: the [profile@]path[#key[,key2]] parser, the profile-resolution rule (explicit > environment override > default), and a single error policy (always set _last_error with the VaultException message; vault() returns null while inline substitution returns empty — both now distinguishable from 'key not found' via _last_error; never silently swallow). Route all four call sites through it, and thread the ScriptContext cancellation token into the inline-expression and function paths (or at minimum funnel their blocking through one adapter) so any future async/retry/caching/audit-logging fix lands in exactly one place instead of four.
user_benefit: Vault failures become diagnosable from scripts regardless of whether they use {{vault:...}}, a vault: step, or vault() — today a script can proceed to push an empty credential to a whole fleet with no recorded reason — and every future Vault behavior change is made once instead of being forgotten on one of four diverging copies.

title: sftp is a second, divergent SSH stack: new connection per step, fully synchronous body, cancellation checked only before connect
existing_state: SftpCommand uses SSH.NET's SftpClient (SftpCommand.cs:5,66) — a completely separate stack from the Rebex SshShellSession/connection pool that powers send. Every sftp step constructs a fresh SftpClient with password-only auth and performs a full TCP connect + key exchange + auth (66-72), then disposes it — so a foreach uploading N files to a host pays N complete SSH handshakes, and a fleet run multiplies that by host count. The entire method is synchronous despite returning Task (ExecuteAsync has zero awaits, 15-103): Connect() (72), UploadFile (82) and DownloadFile (91) all block the worker thread, and the cancellation token is checked exactly once before connecting (64) — pressing Stop during a stuck connect or a large transfer does nothing until OperationTimeout fires (default 120s, 35, or much longer for a slow multi-GB transfer). Capability divergence breeds defects: hosts reachable via send (Rebex pool, key/Vault credentials via CredentialMode.Vault) fail on sftp because only username/password literals or context vars are accepted (111-137), with no key auth and no Vault path.
recommendation: Cache one connected SftpClient per host endpoint on ScriptContext (keyed host:port:user, disposed when the host scope ends) so loops reuse the connection instead of re-handshaking per step. Switch to SSH.NET's async surface: ConnectAsync(cancellationToken), and replace UploadFile/DownloadFile with sftp.Open(...) + Stream.CopyToAsync(buffer, cancellationToken) so Stop actually interrupts transfers. Route credential resolution through the same path the Rebex session uses (per-host vault_path column / CredentialMode.Vault) so sftp and send agree on how a host authenticates. Longer term, evaluate whether Rebex (already licensed and pooled) exposes SFTP so the second stack can be deleted entirely.
user_benefit: Bulk file transfers across a fleet stop paying a full SSH handshake per file, the Stop button works during transfers instead of hanging for up to the timeout, and scripts that authenticate via Vault/keys for send no longer mysteriously fail on sftp steps.

title: Retry temporarily mutates shared step.OnError on the parsed script tree — races under parallel+call, and blocks parallel multi-host execution
existing_state: The retry wrapper writes the per-attempt on_error policy directly onto the parsed step object: `step.OnError = onErrorForAttempt` forcing "stop" on non-final attempts, restored in a finally (Services/Scripting/ScriptExecutor.cs:456-471). ScriptStep instances are shared, not per-execution: the multi-host script path parses once and reuses the same Script object for every host ("Parse the script once", Services/SshExecutionService.cs:505-511, host loop 584-597), loops re-run the same step instances each iteration, ParallelCommand runs child steps concurrently on one context via Task.Run (Services/Scripting/Commands/ParallelCommand.cs:40-61), and ExecuteSubroutineAsync executes the same `definition.Subroutine.Steps` list on every call (ScriptExecutor.cs:656, invoked from CallCommand). So two parallel branches that `call` the same subroutine execute identical ScriptStep objects concurrently — if a step in that subroutine has `retry:` plus `on_error: continue`, one branch's mid-retry "stop" override is visible to the other branch's failure check (~43 commands read the policy via the static `CommandResult.ApplyOnError(step, …)` funnel, IScriptCommand.cs:136-141), silently turning a continue into an abort. AssignStepPaths also writes into the shared tree at every ExecuteAsync start (ScriptExecutor.cs:209-219). Today multi-host runs are sequential (584-597), which masks the cross-host hazard — but this shared-mutable-parse-tree design is exactly what stands in the way of parallelizing fleet runs, the most obvious scaling feature for this app.
recommendation: Stop mutating parsed state. Carry the per-attempt effective on_error out-of-band: e.g., an `AsyncLocal<string?>` override set by ExecuteStepAsync around ExecuteStepCoreAsync and consulted inside `CommandResult.ApplyOnError` (single funnel, so one change covers all ~43 commands), or thread an `effectiveOnError` argument through. For the parallel-multi-host future, add a Script.Clone()/per-host deep copy at run start so each host executes a private tree — that single primitive makes both the retry race and future concurrent host runs safe.
user_benefit: Eliminates a silent error-handling flip (script aborts despite on_error: continue) in parallel+call+retry scripts, and removes the structural landmine standing between this app and parallel multi-host execution.

title: Active host grid has two persisted sources of truth, with a synthetic 'Default' environment papering over the seam
existing_state: Every SaveConfiguration writes the live grid to two places in the same config.json: the active EnvironmentConfig.Hosts (Form1.cs:14630-14633 → EnvironmentService.SaveCurrentGridToEnvironment) and SavedState.Hosts via BuildApplicationState (Form1.cs:14679-14686). Nothing in the model layer ties them together — reconciliation is Form1 convention. The seam is bridged by a synthetic environment: 'Default' is not stored in the Environments map at all until a 'first adoption' event; until then BuildLegacyDefaultEnvironment regenerates it on demand from SavedState (ConfigurationService.cs:202-206, EnvironmentConfig.FromApplicationState:26-46). title: Two near-identical 90-line host-grid loaders and a 4x-duplicated password-migration block that must stay in lockstep

title: Host-grid editing and clipboard logic exists in three diverging copies (Form1, JobEditorDialog, HostGridUtilities) — Form1 got the fast paste, the Job Editor kept the slow one
existing_state: The host grid UX is implemented twice-to-three-times in parallel. title: Two independently maintained hand-rolled YAML step splitters — Flow Canvas Test Step correctness depends on them agreeing
existing_state: Form1.SplitTopLevelYamlSteps (Form1.cs:7458-7531) is a private re-implementation of FlowCanvasBridge.SplitYamlSteps (Services/FlowCanvasBridge.cs:4655+, internal static, same assembly). Both scan for a literal `steps:` line and split on `- ` at the first step indent, but they have already diverged: the bridge version extracts leading-comment runs into comment nodes and strips inline comments (4674-4688), while Form1's version drops comment lines before the first step and glues between-step comment lines onto the PREVIOUS step's snippet (7517-7524). Drift is verified in all three layers today: localcmd's `shell` vocabulary exists in three mutually inconsistent places (editor catalog ["powershell","custom"] at ScriptParser.cs:311; the validation error message "powershell, cmd, custom" at :4985; the actual validator accepting powershell/powershell.exe/cmd/cmd.exe/full paths/custom at :5249-5263) with autocomplete consuming the stale catalog (ScriptAutocompleteProvider.cs:280-289); the parser knows 14 top-level keys including 'preconnect' (:81) but TopLevelKeyDescriptions has 13 — preconnect completes with no description; and "max_seconds" appears twice in the bridge's IntegerOptionKeys (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:174, 182). Two of the hand-sync points fail silently when missed (a container missing its ValidateSteps recursion skips all nested validation; one missing in AssignStepPaths breaks Flow Canvas correlation — both documented prior incidents). The bridge ALREADY queries ScriptParser for option-key catalogs (GetExportOptionKeysByCommand → ScriptParser.GetKnownStepOptionKeysByCommand at 303-315), proving the parser-as-source pattern works — type, required, alias, enum, and description metadata just never moved there.
recommendation: Introduce one per-command descriptor registered next to the parser (name, short description, option keys with type bool/int/list/dict/string + required flag + enum vocabulary, container child-block accessor, handler factory) and derive everything from it: KnownStepKeys/CommandOptionKeys/EnumLikeOptionValuesByCommand, the executor dictionary, generic child-block recursion for ValidateSteps and AssignStepPaths, the editor's description/required/nesting tables (and Form1's tooltip switch), and the bridge's type/required sets (keeping only genuinely presentational data like PreferredOptionOrderOverrides bridge-side). Do it incrementally: phase 1 (cheap, fixes live drift) generates EnumLikeOptionValuesByCommand from the same data the IsValid* validators use and fixes the preconnect/max_seconds gaps; phase 2 unifies child-block traversal so new containers can't silently skip nested validation/step paths; phase 3 folds in dispatch, editor lists, and bridge types. title: Registry stores bare name-to-delegate entries; ~60 handlers hand-roll argument parsing with inconsistent silent failures, blocking validation and autocomplete
existing_state: Every registered function has the shape `object? ScriptFunction(string argsString, ScriptContext context)` — the raw, unsplit argument text (Services/Scripting/Functions/IFunctionCategory.cs:9), and FunctionRegistry stores nothing but the name and delegate (Services/Scripting/FunctionRegistry.cs:25, 37-43). Consequently each handler re-implements the same preamble — JsonUtilities.SplitTopLevelCommas + per-arg resolve + arity check — 63 call sites across 9 files (grep count; e.g. StringFunctions 14, JsonFunctions 15, MathFunctions 7). The hand-rolled arity checks fail inconsistently and always silently: vault() with 1 arg returns null (Services/Scripting/Functions/VaultFunctions.cs:22-23), count() with an unparseable lambda silently degrades to a plain count (Services/Scripting/Functions/CollectionFunctions.cs:130-131), reduce() with a 1-param lambda returns null (CollectionFunctions.cs:67-68), regex_match with 1 arg returns "" while regex_replace with 2 returns null (Services/Scripting/Functions/StringFunctions.cs:159, 182). Because the registry has no arity/signature metadata, ScriptParser validation cannot check function calls, the Scintilla autocomplete provider cannot offer signatures (Services/Editor/ScriptAutocompleteProvider.cs has zero function knowledge), and SCRIPTING.md is hand-maintained with nothing to keep it honest.
recommendation: Extend Register to accept a small FunctionDescriptor (name, min/max arity, param names, category, one-line summary) alongside the delegate — handlers stay untouched, descriptors are added per category class incrementally. Then (a) wrap dispatch so arity violations produce a uniform script warning ('vault() expects 2-3 arguments, got 1') instead of the current per-function null/""/false lottery, (b) feed ScriptAutocompleteProvider and parser-time validation from registry metadata, and (c) optionally generate the SCRIPTING.md function tables from the same source. Do this after (or together with) the function-dispatch consolidation so the metadata covers the full ~112-name surface, not 71.
user_benefit: Wrong-argument-count mistakes — currently the single most common scripting error class, and currently invisible until a fleet run produces empty values — get a clear message, and the editor can finally offer function completion and signature help from a single source of truth.

title: Squiggle positions are regex-scraped from human-readable error strings instead of structured parser output
existing_state: ScriptParser.Validate returns List<string> (ScriptParser.cs:4181-4185) — positions known at validation time are flattened into prose. title: Theming has no single source of truth: duplicate palettes with colliding names, four accent blues, and a dark-mode pixel-brightness heuristic copy-pasted in 10 places
existing_state: Theme colors are defined at least four times. DialogTheme owns the canonical palette (UI/DialogTheme.cs:10-32); Form1 owns a private near-duplicate (Form1.cs:2829-2855) where the SAME constant name means different colors — Form1.DarkSurface1 = (30,30,30) vs DialogTheme.DarkSurface1 = (37,37,38), Form1.DarkSurface2 = (37,37,38) vs DialogTheme.DarkSurface2 = (45,45,46) — and Form1's dark mode has a 4-level surface scale DialogTheme lacks; FindDialog has a third hardcoded palette (FindDialog.cs:9-19); PresetTabHeaderStrip defaults a fourth accent (UI/PresetTabHeaderStrip.cs:35) and is skinned from the Form1 palette (Form1.cs:3388-3394, 3532-3538), not DialogTheme. 'Accent blue' alone exists as (0,120,212) (DialogTheme.LightAccent/DarkAccent, :17,28), (13,110,253) (Form1.LightAccent via GridLightSelection, Form1.cs:2837), (0,122,204) (Form1.DarkSelectionBorder + strip default, :2851), and (0,120,215) (Settings' default custom accent, SettingsDialog.cs:178) — and the user-configurable FontSettings.CustomAccentColor is applied ONLY to btnExecuteSelected (Form1.cs:3316-3328) while DialogTheme.StyleButton paints every primary dialog button with the fixed constant (DialogTheme.cs:197-211). Form1 applies its palette through two parallel ~140-line methods, ApplyLightTheme (3336-3478) and ApplyDarkTheme (3480-3621), that each hand-assign colors to ~50 named controls — so every new control must be wired into both or it ships wrong in one theme; drift has already shipped (the favorites drag-over highlight is hardcoded Color.LightBlue, Form1.cs:5396 — a light-blue blob in dark mode). Because there is no app-level 'current theme' accessor, dialogs guess dark mode from pixel brightness: DialogTheme.ResolveDarkMode reads BackColor.GetBrightness() of the owner or Application.OpenForms[0] (UI/DialogTheme.cs:766-781), and the exact `< 0.2f` heuristic is independently copy-pasted in 8 more dialogs — the six script prompts (ConfirmCommand.cs:118, ChooseCommand.cs:207, InputCommand.cs:180, MultiselectCommand.cs:216, ReadFileCommand.cs:695, WriteFileCommand.cs:729), LocalCmdConfirmationDialog.cs:126, and InteractiveTerminalForm.cs:135 — while BrowserCallbackCaptureCommand diverged to `< 0.5f` (:691, 698), so on a mid-brightness theme the browser-callback prompt themes dark while every other prompt stays light. Several of these theme only when dark and skip the user's dialog font (LocalCmdConfirmationDialog.cs:127-134; NoUpdateDialog/UpdateErrorDialog, UpdateDialog.cs:754-761, constructed without SetDialogFont at Form1.cs:14989/15016 while UpdateDialog itself gets it at 15009). DialogTheme.ApplyTo is also one-way: the dark GroupBox owner-draw Paint lambda is added and never removed (DialogTheme.cs:92-120), so re-applying stacks handlers and can never revert to light — unlike StyleTabControl's correct -=/+= (368-370, 403-404). Two raw MessageBox.Show calls survive in the Vault Test Connection handler (SettingsDialog.cs:1069, 1073) despite the file's themed _promptService (used at 2445, 2766).
recommendation: Introduce a single static theme source — DialogTheme.IsDarkMode (plus CurrentFont and one Accent token reading FontSettings.CustomAccentColor when set) — set once by Form1 when config loads and on theme change. Delete ResolveDarkMode's brightness guess and all 9 copy-pasted heuristics (each dialog just calls DialogTheme.ApplyTo(this, DialogTheme.IsDarkMode), which also gives those dialogs light-mode theming and the dialog font for free). Merge the palettes: promote Form1's richer tokens (4-level surface scale, selection border) into DialogTheme as named semantic tokens, rename the colliding DarkSurfaceN constants so one name means one color, and delete the Form1/FindDialog constants. Collapse ApplyLightTheme/ApplyDarkTheme into one ApplyTheme(ThemePalette p) pass driven by a palette struct so each control is themed in exactly one line; replace the Color.LightBlue drag highlight at 5396 with the shared selection token. Make ApplyTo's GroupBox styling re-appliable (named handler, -= then +=), have StyleButton and Form1 both read the single accent token, and route the two MessageBox.Show stragglers through _promptService.
user_benefit: Stops the steady drip of one-theme-only visual bugs this structure already produces — mismatched accent blues between the main window/dialogs/tab strip, a light-blue drag highlight in dark mode, unthemed light-mode prompts, dialogs disagreeing about dark mode in the same run — and makes any future palette change or third theme a one-place edit instead of a hunt through two 140-line methods and ten heuristic sites.

title: SettingsDialog is a 2,812-line god class bound together by stringly-typed control lookups
existing_state: SettingsDialog.cs is a single 2,812-line class containing six CreateXxxTab builder methods, two full profile-manager subsystems, the appearance preview engine, and one monolithic BtnSave_Click that writes ~60 settings across every tab (2657-2755). Its ~60 control fields are hydrated after construction by 34 recursive name-string lookups — FindControl<T>(tab, "chkRememberState") etc. (bindings from line 276) — where FindControl returns null! on a miss (2308-2317): renaming a control's Name string compiles cleanly and produces a NullReferenceException at first use, far from the cause, with zero compile-time safety. Do it one tab at a time (General and Updates are trivial starters); the existing SettingsDialogVaultTests/AppearanceTests exercising the internal ctor keep the refactor honest.
user_benefit: Settings work stops being high-risk: new options become localized, compile-checked changes instead of edits to a 2,800-line form where a renamed string detonates at runtime — and it unblocks making the dialog resizable.

title: Main-form lock during script prompts hinges on the magic control name "btnStopAll" and silently no-ops if it's missing
